title: How Billionaires Pay Less Tax Than You (Legally)
sources: ProPublica, 'The Secret IRS Files' (June 2021): 25 richest Americans' wealth grew $401B (2014–2018) while paying $13.6B in federal income tax — a 'true tax rate' of 3.4%
U.S. Census Bureau: median household income $83,730 (2024)
IRS 2026 brackets: 10%–37%; long-term capital gains rates 0% / 15% / 20% (+3.8% net investment income tax for high earners)
Step-up in basis at death: Congressional Research Service IF11812; CBO budget options; Tax Policy Center
Estate tax: 40% top rate above ≈ $15 million per person exemption (2026)
Warren Buffett, 'Stop Coddling the Super-Rich', New York Times (Aug 14, 2011): 17.4% of taxable income vs 33%–41% for his office staff
Tax Foundation / IRS data (2022): top 1% of earners paid ≈ 40% of all federal income taxes
U.S. federal corporate income tax rate: 21% (since 2018)

beats.text: Dave earns sixty thousand dollars a year. Before his paycheck even reaches him, taxes are taken out. About one dollar out of every six.
Now look at this. A few years ago, a news investigation looked at the tax records of the twenty five richest Americans.
In five years, their wealth grew by four hundred and one billion dollars. The income tax they paid? Just thirteen point six billion.
That's a true tax rate of about three point four percent. Dave pays way more than that.
And here's the crazy part. It's mostly legal.
Today: the simple three step trick called buy, borrow, die. Why it works. And the arguments on both sides.
First, let's see how Dave pays.
Dave works at an office. Every two weeks, his boss pays him. And before the money lands in his account, the government takes its slice.
Some goes to income tax. Some goes to Social Security and Medicare. Dave doesn't choose. He doesn't wait. It just happens.
Why? Because Dave's money comes as a salary. And a salary is income. And income gets taxed right away.
Remember that word. Income. Because the whole trick is about avoiding it.
Over a whole year, that's roughly ten thousand dollars that Dave never even touches. It leaves before it arrives.
Meet Richie. Richie started a company. He owns ten billion dollars of its shares.
Richie's salary? One dollar a year. Some famous billionaires really do this.
This year, the company does great. Richie's shares go up by one billion dollars. He is one billion dollars richer.
How much tax does he pay on that billion? Zero.
Because in the tax rules, that billion isn't income yet. It's a gain on paper. It only counts when he sells the shares.
Think of an apple tree. You only pay tax on the apples you pick. But the tree itself can grow bigger and bigger, and nobody taxes the tree.
Dave gets paid in apples. Richie owns the tree.
So here's the three step trick. Step one: buy.
Buy things that grow in value. Shares of companies. Buildings. Land. Whole businesses.
And then, the most important rule: never sell them. Because selling is what creates income. And income creates tax.
If Richie sold one billion dollars of shares, he could owe around twenty four percent in federal tax on the gain. So he doesn't sell.
But wait. If Richie never sells anything, how does he pay for his yacht?
Step two: borrow.
Richie walks into a bank and says: I need fifty million dollars. And I'll use my shares as a guarantee.
The bank loves this. The shares are worth billions. The risk is tiny. So they give Richie a loan, often at a low interest rate.
And here's the key. A loan is not income. You have to pay it back. So there's no income tax on borrowed money.
Richie pays some interest to the bank. But that interest is usually far less than the tax he'd pay if he sold.
And while he spends the loan, his shares keep growing. Often faster than the interest. So he can keep borrowing, year after year.
It's like living off an apple tree without ever picking an apple. You just borrow apples from the neighbor, and promise him the tree.
And remember our very first video? When a bank makes a loan, it creates new money. So the bank is happy, Richie is happy, and the tax office gets nothing.
And step three. Well. Die.
Sorry, Richie. But this is where the magic happens.
When Richie passes away, his kids inherit the shares. Normally, if you sell shares, you pay tax on the growth since you bought them.
But there's a rule called the step up in basis. When you inherit something, the tax clock resets. It's treated as if your kids bought the shares on the day Richie died.
So all the growth during Richie's whole life? For income tax, it simply vanishes. Poof.
The kids can sell some shares, pay back Richie's loans, and owe little or no income tax on decades of growth.
Now, there is an estate tax. Up to forty percent on very large estates. But the richest families hire experts, and use special trusts to shrink that bill a lot.
Even some billionaires think this is strange.
In twenty eleven, Warren Buffett, one of the richest people alive, wrote an article in The New York Times.
He said that the year before, he paid about seventeen percent of his taxable income in federal taxes.
And the people working in his office? They paid between thirty three and forty one percent.
Why? Because most of Buffett's money came from investments, and gains on investments are taxed at lower rates than salaries. His staff earned salaries.
One of the richest men in the world, paying a lower rate than his own staff. And he was asking to pay more.
Now, to be fair, there's another side to this story. And smart people disagree.
Argument one: taxing paper gains is tricky. Shares can crash. Imagine paying tax on a billion dollar gain, and then the next year, the gain is gone.
Argument two: the company already pays tax on its profits. In America, corporations pay twenty one percent. So some say, taxing the owner again is taxing twice.
Argument three: high earners already pay a huge share. The top one percent of earners pay around forty percent of all federal income taxes.
And the other side answers: a percentage of a huge fortune is still small, and ordinary workers can't borrow against billions to avoid paying.
Should the rules change? That's a political question. But now you know how the rules actually work.
So can Dave use any of this? A little. The same ideas work in small ways. Education, not advice.
One. Own things that grow, not just a salary. Even small investments can grow without being taxed every year.
Two. Be patient. In America, if you hold an investment for more than one year before selling, the tax rate on the gain is usually lower. For many people, it can even be zero.
Three. Use tax friendly accounts, like a four oh one k or an I R A, where investments can grow with less tax.
And four. The step up rule isn't only for billionaires. If Dave ever inherits Grandma's house, it applies to him too.
So let's recap.
One. Salaries are taxed right away. Growing wealth is not taxed until you sell.
Two. The very rich buy things that grow, borrow against them instead of selling, and pass them on when they die.
Three. It's legal, it's debated, and both sides have real arguments.
